title: 5 Essential Navigation Patterns for UX
summary: This reel explains when and how to use five common navigation patterns: bottom tabs, sidebars, hamburger menus, command palettes, and breadcrumbs. It provides specific rules for mobile versus desktop and highlights common pitfalls to avoid to ensure better user retention.

transcript.text: 5 nav patterns. Pick wrong, lose users.
Bottom tabs. Mobile only. 3 to 5 top-level destinations max.
Beyond 5, users can't parse what's there. Always visible, always thumb-reachable.
Sidebar. Desktop only. Use it when content is hierarchical or when you have more than 5 sections.
Persistent, collapsible, but never hidden behind a click.
Hamburger. Mobile only. Secondary content. Settings, account, support.
Never your primary navigation. Studies show 40% fewer users click hidden menus.
Command palette. Power users only. Cmd K opens search-driven navigation.
Linear, Notion, Raycast. Never your primary nav for new users. They don't know it exists.
Breadcrumbs. Only when hierarchy goes deeper than 2 levels.
They show position, not navigation. Don't ship them in a flat structure. They confuse more than they help.
Mobile equals tabs. Desktop equals sidebar. Everything else has a specific job. Save this for your next IA decision.

design_principles: Limit bottom tabs to 3-5 items for mobile visibility and reachability.
Use sidebars for desktop when content is hierarchical or exceeds 5 sections.
Reserve hamburger menus for secondary content on mobile; avoid them for primary navigation.
Command palettes are shortcuts for power users, not a replacement for primary navigation.
Use breadcrumbs only for hierarchies deeper than 2 levels to show position, not as a primary navigation tool.
